sections.title: Stage 6 skills
sections.description: Research, analysis, evaluation, reflection, collaboration and communication — the six thinking skills you grew in Stage 6.

sections.title: Research and Analysis
sections.description: The research and analysis skills you built in Stage 4 — asking good questions, checking sources, spotting patterns and telling fact from opinion.

sections.title: Foundations (Stages 3–4)
sections.description: Early teamwork, fairness and finding-out skills from Stages 3 and 4.

questions.question: Ayan is researching how learners travel to school. Which of these is a LOCAL question?
questions.options: How do learners in my town travel to school? | How do children travel to school around the world? | How do learners across my whole country travel to school? | Why do people travel at all?
questions.correctAnswer: How do learners in my town travel to school?
questions.explanation: A local question points at your own town or neighbourhood. Questions about the whole country are national, and questions about the world are global.

questions.question: Before his survey, Hamza writes: 'I think most of my classmates will choose football as their favourite sport.' What is this statement?
questions.options: A source he found on a website | A prediction he can test by gathering answers | A conclusion drawn from evidence | A fact that is already proven
questions.correctAnswer: A prediction he can test by gathering answers
questions.explanation: A prediction is a smart guess about what you think you will find. It only becomes a conclusion after the evidence is gathered and checked.

questions.question: Layla asked 30 learners the same question and now has a big pile of answers. What is the tidiest way to record them?
questions.options: Try to remember them all in her head | Write one long paragraph containing every answer | Draw a picture of her school | Count the answers in a tally chart
questions.correctAnswer: Count the answers in a tally chart
questions.explanation: A tally chart records lots of answers neatly, so you can count each choice at a glance instead of hunting through a jumble of words.

questions.question: Yusuf surveyed 30 learners at his school and 24 said they drink water at lunch. Which conclusion does his evidence let him draw?
questions.options: Nobody at his school drinks milk | Most of the learners he surveyed drink water at lunch | Every child in the country drinks water at lunch | Water is the tastiest drink in the world
questions.correctAnswer: Most of the learners he surveyed drink water at lunch
questions.explanation: A conclusion is only as big as the evidence behind it. Yusuf asked 30 learners at one school, so he can speak about them — not about every child in the country.

questions.question: Which of these statements is a FACT?
questions.options: Rainy days are boring | Our school has 400 students | Football is the best sport | Mango juice tastes better than orange juice
questions.correctAnswer: Our school has 400 students
questions.explanation: A fact can be checked and shown to be true — you could count the students. The other statements are opinions about what someone likes or feels.

questions.question: A town plans to build a new market on the football field. Who is a STAKEHOLDER in this issue?
questions.options: A character in a storybook | Nobody, because the market is not built yet | The children who play football on the field | A person far away who has never heard of the town
questions.correctAnswer: The children who play football on the field
questions.explanation: A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in an issue. The children would lose their playing field, so the plan truly affects them.

questions.question: After the bins were removed from the park, litter on the grass increased. What is the most likely CAUSE of the extra litter?
questions.options: The name of the park | The extra litter on the grass | The colour of the park gates | The removal of the bins
questions.correctAnswer: The removal of the bins
questions.explanation: A cause is the reason something happens. With no bins, people had nowhere to put their rubbish — the extra litter is the consequence.

questions.question: Four people wrote about rubbish near the river. Which sentence shows the STRONGEST feeling?
questions.options: This dumping is a disgrace and it must stop now | The river is about two metres wide | Some rubbish has been left near the river | The report about the river came out in May
questions.correctAnswer: This dumping is a disgrace and it must stop now
questions.explanation: Words like 'disgrace' and 'must stop now' are strong, persuasive words. They show the writer feels very strongly, while the other sentences stay calm and neutral.

questions.question: Zahra reads an advert that says a fizzy drink is 'the healthiest drink in the world'. What should she remember about this source?
questions.options: The drink must be healthy because the advert says so | It was made to sell the drink, so it may not be balanced | Adverts are always true | Adverts never talk about drinks
questions.correctAnswer: It was made to sell the drink, so it may not be balanced
questions.explanation: Every source is made for a purpose. An advert's purpose is to sell, so it shows only the good side — a careful evaluator keeps that in mind.

questions.question: Idil wants to know how much rain fell in her region last year. Which source is MOST useful for her goal?
questions.options: A poem about the rainy season | An advert for umbrellas | The national weather service's rainfall records | A friend's memory of one rainy afternoon
questions.correctAnswer: The national weather service's rainfall records
questions.explanation: A source is useful when it matches your goal. The weather service measures rainfall carefully all year, so its records answer exactly what Idil is asking.

questions.question: Four sources talk about looking after your teeth. Which author has the most EXPERTISE?
questions.options: A comment online with no name on it | A guess from someone who has never studied teeth | An advert made by a sweet company | A dentist writing for a health website
questions.correctAnswer: A dentist writing for a health website
questions.explanation: Expertise means the maker really knows the subject. A dentist has studied and cared for teeth for years, so their advice deserves more trust.

questions.question: Nashad's source is a photograph of a flooded street. Photographs have strengths, but what is one LIMITATION of this source?
questions.options: It lists the rainfall for the whole year | It cannot tell her why the flood happened | It proves floods happen in every town | It shows nothing useful at all
questions.correctAnswer: It cannot tell her why the flood happened
questions.explanation: A photograph shows one real moment — that is its strength. Its limitation is what it cannot do: it cannot explain causes or show what happened before or after.

questions.question: After a team project, which sentence belongs in a BALANCED reflection?
questions.options: Our poster went well, but our planning was slow, so next time we will plan first | I cannot remember anything about the project | Everything was perfect and there is nothing to improve | It was all my teammates' fault
questions.correctAnswer: Our poster went well, but our planning was slow, so next time we will plan first
questions.explanation: A balanced reflection is honest about what went well AND what could be better, and it says what you will change next time.

questions.question: In her team's project, Aisha collected the survey answers and typed up the results. What do we call the part she played?
questions.options: Her questionnaire | Her prediction | Her source | Her contribution to the team
questions.correctAnswer: Her contribution to the team
questions.explanation: Your contribution is the work you personally do to help the team. A strong reflection names your contribution clearly.

questions.question: Before his project, Omar thought all plastic gets recycled. His research showed that most of it does not. What is the best way for him to reflect on this?
questions.options: I was right all along, so the research does not matter | I will stop thinking about plastic | My research changed my mind: I learned that most plastic is not recycled | Research never changes what people think
questions.correctAnswer: My research changed my mind: I learned that most plastic is not recycled
questions.explanation: The deepest reflection notices how new information changed your thinking. Changing your mind because of good evidence is a strength, not a mistake.

questions.question: A new team is about to start a project together. What should the team agree on FIRST?
questions.options: Who gets to talk the most | The shared outcome they are all working towards | The colour of everyone's pencils | Which teammate to blame if it goes wrong
questions.correctAnswer: The shared outcome they are all working towards
questions.explanation: Every strong team starts by agreeing its shared outcome — the one result everyone is working towards. Then all the jobs and plans can point at it.

questions.question: Maryam draws beautifully and Daud is confident speaking to the class. Their team must make a poster and present it. What is the FAIREST way to divide the tasks?
questions.options: Daud does both jobs on his own | They both wait for the teacher to do it | Maryam does both jobs because she is older | Maryam designs the poster and Daud gives the presentation
questions.correctAnswer: Maryam designs the poster and Daud gives the presentation
questions.explanation: Fair teams divide tasks by each person's skill. Giving the drawing to the artist and the talking to the confident speaker uses everyone's strengths.

questions.question: Two teammates disagree about which idea to choose for their project. What is a FRIENDLY way to resolve the disagreement?
questions.options: Listen to both ideas, then decide together, perhaps with a vote | Shout until one person gives up | Stop having ideas altogether | Leave the team and work alone
questions.correctAnswer: Listen to both ideas, then decide together, perhaps with a vote
questions.explanation: Disagreements are normal in every team. Listening to each idea and deciding together keeps the team friendly and often finds the best plan.

questions.question: Before giving her talk, Nasra writes a short plan showing the beginning, middle and end. What is this plan called?
questions.options: A skeleton plan | A prediction | A questionnaire | A tally chart
questions.correctAnswer: A skeleton plan
questions.explanation: A skeleton plan is the simple 'bones' of a talk — beginning, middle and end — so the presentation does not wander and lose its audience.

questions.question: Sagal found seven arguments for her case, but her talk only has time for three. What should she do?
questions.options: Choose her three strongest arguments and support them with evidence | Read all seven arguments as fast as she can | Give the talk with no arguments at all | Pick three arguments without thinking about them
questions.correctAnswer: Choose her three strongest arguments and support them with evidence
questions.explanation: A good communicator selects only the most persuasive arguments. A few powerful, well-supported points convince people more than a rushed list.

questions.question: During his talk, Khalid says: 'According to the national health survey, one in three children skips breakfast.' Why is this good communication?
questions.options: It makes the talk longer | It hides where his information came from | Surveys always sound clever | He refers to his source, so listeners can trust and check his information
questions.correctAnswer: He refers to his source, so listeners can trust and check his information
questions.explanation: Referring to your sources shows your information is not made up. Listeners can trust it more, and they can go and check it for themselves.

questions.question: Which sentence clearly STATES A POSITION on an issue?
questions.options: Some people sometimes talk about recycling | What is recycling? | Recycling is a word in the dictionary | I believe our school should recycle more, and here are my reasons
questions.correctAnswer: I believe our school should recycle more, and here are my reasons
questions.explanation: Stating your position means saying clearly where you stand on an issue — and a persuasive speaker follows it with reasons and evidence.

questions.question: Which of these is an OPEN question — one that invites a long, interesting answer?
questions.options: Are you ten years old? | Is today Monday? | Why do you enjoy your favourite game? | Do you like football?
questions.correctAnswer: Why do you enjoy your favourite game?
questions.explanation: An open question cannot be answered with just 'yes' or 'no'. 'Why' and 'how' questions invite people to explain, which gives researchers much richer answers.

questions.question: Warda finds a website about healthy food. Before she uses it, what should she check FIRST?
questions.options: What colour the website is | How long the web address is | Who made the website and whether they know the subject | Whether the website has funny pictures
questions.correctAnswer: Who made the website and whether they know the subject
questions.explanation: Good researchers check a source before trusting it. Asking who made it, and whether they really know the subject, tells you how much to trust what it says.

questions.question: Abdi is taking notes from a library book for his project. What should he do?
questions.options: Only copy the page numbers | Write down nothing and hope to remember | Write short reminders of the key ideas in his own words | Copy every sentence from the book exactly
questions.correctAnswer: Write short reminders of the key ideas in his own words
questions.explanation: Notes are short reminders in your own words. Writing ideas your own way helps you understand them — copying whole sentences does not.

questions.question: Hodan counted how her classmates travel to school. What is the CLEAREST way to share what she found?
questions.options: Whisper the results to one friend | Throw the answers away | Show the counts in a simple chart or table | Keep the answers secret in her notebook
questions.correctAnswer: Show the counts in a simple chart or table
questions.explanation: Findings are only useful if others can understand them. A simple chart or table lets everyone see the results at a glance.

questions.question: A farmer is happy about a rainy day, but a bus driver is worried about it. Why do they think differently about the same rain?
questions.options: Rain is impossible to think about | They secretly agree with each other | They have different perspectives, because the rain affects each of them differently | One of them must be lying about the rain
questions.correctAnswer: They have different perspectives, because the rain affects each of them differently
questions.explanation: A perspective is a person's way of seeing things. Rain waters the farmer's crops but makes the driver's roads slippery — so each sees the same day differently, and both are honest.

questions.question: Which of these statements is an OPINION?
questions.options: School mornings are the best part of the day | Our class has 25 learners | The market opens at 8 o'clock | Water turns to ice when it freezes
questions.correctAnswer: School mornings are the best part of the day
questions.explanation: An opinion is what someone thinks or feels, and different people can disagree about it. The other statements can all be checked and shown to be true.

questions.question: The library counted its visitors: Monday 4, Tuesday 8, Wednesday 12, Thursday 16. What PATTERN do the numbers show?
questions.options: The number of visitors grows by 4 each day | The numbers show no pattern at all | The library is closed on Thursdays | The visitors get fewer every day
questions.correctAnswer: The number of visitors grows by 4 each day
questions.explanation: A pattern is something the data keeps doing. Each day the count rises by 4 — spotting patterns like this is the heart of analysing data.

questions.question: The school tap was left running all night, so the yard was flooded in the morning. What is the CAUSE in this story?
questions.options: The tap being left running | The morning bell | The school gate | The flooded yard
questions.correctAnswer: The tap being left running
questions.explanation: The cause is what made it happen: the running tap. The flooded yard is the effect — the thing that happened because of it.

questions.question: A team of friends is building a model bridge together. What helps the team work well?
questions.options: Nobody helps with the building | Everyone shouts their ideas at the same time | Everyone has a job and listens to each other | One person does everything alone
questions.correctAnswer: Everyone has a job and listens to each other
questions.explanation: Good teams share the jobs and listen to every member. That way everyone helps, and the bridge gets built together.

questions.question: A playground rule says only the tallest child may ever have a turn on the swing. What is the best thing to say about this rule?
questions.options: Only grown-ups should use swings | It is not fair, because everyone should get a turn | Rules do not matter in a playground | It is fair, because tall children need more turns
questions.correctAnswer: It is not fair, because everyone should get a turn
questions.explanation: A fair rule treats everyone the same. This rule leaves most children out, so it is not fair — good rules give everybody a turn.

questions.question: Which of these is a NEED — something everyone must have — rather than a want?
questions.options: Clean drinking water | A gold watch | A new video game | Sweets every day
questions.correctAnswer: Clean drinking water
questions.explanation: A need is something people must have to live and stay healthy, like clean water. Games, watches and sweets are wants — nice to have, but not needed to live.

questions.question: Musa is starting an investigation. Which step comes FIRST?
questions.options: Draw a pictogram of his results | Present his results to the class | Choose the question he wants to answer | Write his conclusion
questions.correctAnswer: Choose the question he wants to answer
questions.explanation: An investigation follows steps in order, and it always starts with a question. Only after asking and gathering answers can you draw results and conclusions.

questions.question: Fatima's team has just finished their project. What does it mean for her to REFLECT on it?
questions.options: Blame a teammate for the hard parts | Do the same project again without thinking | Forget the project straight away | Think about what went well and what could be better next time
questions.correctAnswer: Think about what went well and what could be better next time
questions.explanation: Reflecting means looking back honestly at your work — celebrating what went well and spotting what to improve — so the next project goes even better.

questions.question: Faisal wants to persuade his class to keep the playground tidy. Which sentence will persuade them BEST?
questions.options: I have no reason, but tidy up anyway | Tidying is a word I know | Just do it because I said so | We should keep it tidy, because a clean playground is safer and nicer for everyone
questions.correctAnswer: We should keep it tidy, because a clean playground is safer and nicer for everyone
questions.explanation: Persuading people works best when you give a reason. Saying WHY the idea helps everyone makes people want to join in.
